findings.title: A 64-bit instance hash deduplicated across packages with no check: a crafted collision is one body for two layouts
findings.program:
# package d (an adversary's dependency: two spellings whose first 16 hex digits of BLAKE3 agree,
# found in about 2^32 trials, which is minutes)
pub struct A: x: i64
pub struct B: x: i64, y: i64, z: i64
pub fn grow(ref mut xs: Array[A]):
    xs.push(owns A(x=1))            # d instantiates Array[A].push: em_3std4core5Array4pushG<h>
pub fn feed(ref mut xs: Array[B]): pass

# root package
from d import B, feed
fn main():
    xs: Array[B] = []
    xs.push(owns B(x=1, y=2, z=3))  # the root instantiates Array[B].push: the same symbol em_...G<h>
    feed(ref mut xs)                # <-- link-time dedup keeps one body for both: 24-byte elements written by the 8-byte body (or the reverse); out of bounds in safe code
findings.why: [MNG-1]: "for a generic instance `G` and the first 16 hex digits of the BLAKE3 hash of the canonical spelling of its arguments" and "A hash collision between two instances is reported as `E9040`, naming both": only a compiler that sees both instances can report it. [MONO-1]: "instances are named deterministically ... and deduplicated at link time, across separately compiled packages too": the link step compares names, never spellings. Nothing says the spelling travels with the symbol.
findings.proposed_text: * `[MNG-1]` replace "A hash collision between two instances is reported as `E9040`, naming both, never as an internal error." with: "The hash is 32 hex digits (128 bits), so that no two spellings a program can write collide by chance or by design. Beside each instance's symbol the package records the canonical spelling it hashed, in its interface file and in the object's manifest section; before the linker runs, the build compares the spellings of every instance symbol two packages both define, and two that differ are `E9040`, naming both spellings and both packages, never an internal error and never one body for two instances. Within one package the same compare runs when the instance is named."
findings.codes: E9040, raised at the build's link step as well as in the compiler; shape: name and type (XVII.6.2)
findings.milestone: M15 (mangling, A7-16), with the link step of M-C's library build

# geometry v1: pub struct Vec2: x: f64, y: f64
# geometry v2: pub struct Vec2: x: f64, y: f64, w: f64        (both majors coexist, [VER-5])

findings.title: The copy for one whole variable under two names needs a callee body the caller may not have
findings.program:
# package lib (compiled once)
pub fn add_both(ref mut a: int, ref mut b: int):
    a += 1
    b += 1
    println(a)

# root
from lib import add_both
fn main():
    x = 0
    add_both(ref mut x, ref mut x)   # <-- accepted by [BCK-5] (one whole variable proved); [MONO-10] compiles it "against its own copy of the callee", whose body the root never has
    f: fn(ref mut int, ref mut int) = add_both
    f(ref mut x, ref mut x)          # <-- which callee's copy? a function value may hold any function
findings.why: [MONO-10]: "is compiled against its own copy of the callee in which the two names are one place"; [BCK-5]: "two of them ... name one place ... only where the compiler proves them one whole variable (`[MONO-10]`)". Across a package's edge only summaries ([EFF-4]) and inline bodies ([CG-C-3]) travel; a `pub` function of over 40 statements, one with a foreign call, an `extern` function, and any call through a function value, interface, `dyn` or `virtual` method have no body to copy. The compiler must invent whether to refuse or to require the body.
findings.proposed_text: * `[MONO-10]` append: "The copy is compiled by the caller's package from the callee's body: for a function of its own package, from the source; for a `pub` function of another package, from that package's interface file, which carries (as `[CG-C-3]`'s header carries inline bodies, `[CG-C-3b]`) the body of every `pub` function that has two or more `ref mut` parameters, or one `ref mut` parameter and a `pub static mut` it uses by name. Where no body can be had — a call through a function value, an interface, `dyn` or `virtual` method, or of an `extern` function — a call that names one whole variable twice is `E3022` (\"`f(ref mut x, ref mut x)` names `x` twice, and `f` may hold any function, which has no copy for one variable; call the function by name, `add_both(ref mut x, ref mut x)`, or give the second name a value of its own: `y = x` above the call and `f(ref mut x, ref mut y)`\")."

findings.title: extends O1: a dependant's implementation, override or stored function flows into a library's already-checked call
findings.program:
# package lib (compiled once; no Visitor it has ends a Node, so `walk` keeps plain views)
pub interface Visitor:
    fn visit(this, n: Node)
pub class Tree:
    nodes: Array[owns Node]
    pub fn walk(this, v: dyn Visitor):
        for n in this.nodes:
            v.visit(n)                 # checked against the union of implementations lib can see

# package app
from lib import Tree, Visitor, Node
class Pruner implements Visitor:
    tree: shares mut Tree
    fn visit(this, n: Node):
        this.tree.nodes.clear()        # <-- ends every Node while lib's `walk` still holds the view `n`: use after free; nothing re-checks `walk`
fn main():
    t = shares mut Tree(nodes=[owns Node()])
    t.walk(Pruner(tree=shares mut t))
findings.why: [EFF-2]: "For an interface, `dyn` or `virtual` method, it is every implementation and override the program has"; [BCK-8]: "the union of the summaries of every function the program can put there ... Summaries are the least fixed point over the whole program's call graph": a whole-program fact. [BLD-14] point 7 and [EFF-4] record the *library's* stores for its dependants; nothing records what the library's own lines relied on, and [BLD-2] re-checks a module only when what it imports changes. The same holds for a function the dependant stores into a library's `pub` field of function type and for an override of a `pub virtual` method. AUDIT O1 lists [OBJ-1], [THR-2], [WK-18]; this is the same shape for [BCK-8].
findings.proposed_text: * `[BLD-14]` add point 8: "for each call through a `pub` interface or `virtual` method, or through a `pub` place of function type (a field, a parameter, an element), the facts the package's own checks relied on at that call: what the functions there may change, read and end, as `[HR-44]` records them for a reload. A package that adds to such a place — an implementation of the interface, an override, a function it stores there or passes to it — is checked against them when it compiles: an implementation, override or store whose summary breaks a fact a recorded line relied on is refused at its own line, with the code of the rule that line relied on (`E3020`, `E3021`, `E3031` or `E3060`), naming the library's line and the chain of calls (\"`Pruner.visit` clears `tree.nodes`, and `lib`'s `Tree.walk` (lib/tree.em line 7) walks `nodes` across its call of `visit`; keep what to remove in a list of your own and clear after the walk\"). So no package's accepted line is made unsafe by a package it never saw, and nothing runs for it while the program runs."
findings.codes: E3020, E3021, E3031, E3060 at the dependant's line; interface-file entries

findings.title: The home count is folded into the away count unchecked: a count past half the range wraps
findings.program:
from std.thread import thread
class Log: pass
fn main():
    log = thread_shared Log()
    holders: Array[thread_shared Log] = []
    for i in 0..3_000_000_000:                              # every +1 passes the home count's compare (its limit is 4,294,967,295)
        holders.push(owns thread_shared log)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared log: pass)     # <-- a hand-over ([RC-4] point 4): the making thread adds its 3,000,000,000 into the away count, a signed 32-bit number whose limit is 2,147,483,647, with no compare: it wraps negative
    h.join()                                                # the sum is read as zero or below: the Log ends under 3,000,000,000 live owners
findings.why: [RT-7]: "A `thread_shared` value's home count (`[RC-4]`) is checked as a one-thread count is" (limit 4,294,967,295) while "its away count ... the program stops when the value before the add is at or above 2,147,483,647". [RC-4] point 4: "first adds its own count of the value into the away count"; point 2: "it adds each value's home count into its away count". Neither add is named among the checked ones; a home count above 2,147,483,647 cannot fit.
findings.proposed_text: * `[RT-7]` append: "The add of a home count into the away count — at a hand-over (`[RC-4]` point 4) and at the queue's emptying (point 2) — is checked as a +1 is: when the sum would be 2,147,483,647 or more, the program stops with the same message (\"too many owners of a `Log` (2,147,483,647)\"); one compare per hand-over or per queued value, never on the fast path. The 8-bit test program reaches it at 127."
findings.codes: the stop text of [RT-7]; the `[COST-3]` row for the hand-over gains "and one compare"

findings.title: A thread at depth zero may enter Ember code during commit and run through a half-rewritten image
findings.why: [HR-3]: "applied only ... when no registered thread is executing Ember code (each thread's Ember-depth counter is zero)" states the condition at the moment of the read, not for the length of commit. [HR-42]: "Commit reads every counter with acquire, writes the new thunk targets and type information, and publishes them with one release store"; [HR-42a]: "The counter is not a lock: entering Ember code is one relaxed increment and one acquire fence". A relaxed increment and an acquire fence on one side and an acquire read on the other do not order the two (no Dekker), and nothing makes an entering thread wait.
findings.proposed_text:
* `[HR-42]` replace with: "**Publication.** Entering Ember code increments the thread's depth counter and then reads the runtime's commit mark, both sequentially consistent (one full fence between them where the hardware needs it); a thread that reads the mark set decrements its counter, waits until the reload generation counter changes, and enters again. Leaving Ember code is a release decrement. Commit sets the commit mark and then reads every counter, with the same ordering, so that of a thread entering and a commit starting at once at least one sees the other; a counter that is not zero clears the mark and the poll returns `EMBER_RELOAD_UNSAFE_POINT`. With every counter zero, commit writes the instances, the type information and the call table, publishes them with one release store to the generation counter, which a thread entering next acquires, and clears the mark."
* `[HR-42a]` replace with: "The counter is not a lock: entering Ember code is one increment, one fence and one load whatever the number of threads; only a thread that meets a commit waits, for the length of the commit, and the reload side pays the scan over threads."
findings.codes: none; a `[COST-3]` row: entering Ember code from C in a reloadable build, one increment, one fence, one load

findings.title: A frame's view into a field of an instance migrated in place is neither rewritten nor counted as a dependence
findings.program:
class Player:
    hp: int
    name: String

fn run(ref mut p: Player):
    hp = ref mut p.hp            # a view into a field
    std.hot.checkpoint()         # the edit adds `armor: int = 0` before `hp`; the new size fits, so the instance keeps its address
    hp += 1                      # <-- the rest of `run` reads or writes no field of `Player`: it writes through an `int` view at the old offset, now `armor` or half of `name`
findings.why: [HR-3b]: a frame depends on "the types whose layout the rest of the function depends on once the call returns: those its old code reads or writes fields of, builds, holds, passes or gets back by value, indexes or allocates" — after the call the old code holds a `ref mut int`, not a `Player`; whether "holds" reaches through a view is the compiler's guess. [HR-3b]: "one a frame's view points into keeps its address, which `[HR-15]` allows when its new size fits" — the address is kept, the field moved. [HR-15a] refuses only what "must move"; "a frame's views are not counted".
findings.proposed_text: * `[HR-3b]` after "the types whose layout the rest of the function depends on once the call returns:" insert: "those a value it still uses is of, holds, or views — a view into a field, an element or a part depends on the type that holds the part and on every type on the path to it, read from the places the view carries (`[BCK-1]`);". And replace "one a frame's view points into keeps its address, which `[HR-15]` allows when its new size fits" with "an instance a frame's view points into is not changed in place while that frame lives: a layout change of its type is a dependence of the frame, and is refused naming the function, the line of its call and the view".

findings.title: A kept view into a field that migration removes, converts or moves within its block is rewritten to the wrong place or to nothing
findings.why: [HR-15]: "commit rewrites every owner, link and view of it that the runtime can enumerate: ... the kept views into it (`ref T`, `ref mut T`, ...)" — a view of *it*, with no word on a view into a part of it, whose offset changes by name ("fields reordered | carried over by name") or whose part is "field removed | old value ended in reclaim" or converted ("field type widened losslessly | converted"). No row of [HR-14] and no sentence of [HR-15a] refuses a reload whose migration leaves a kept view without its part.
findings.proposed_text: * `[HR-15c]` *(new)* "**A view into a part.** A kept view (`[TYP-15]`) that points into a part of a value — a field, an element, a range of a `String` or an array — is rewritten to the part's new place when the part is carried over by name (reordered, its holder resized or moved): the runtime maps the old offset to the new through the schema. Where the part is removed, converted, rebuilt by `migrate_from`, or of a type whose own layout changes, the view has no place to be rewritten to, and plan refuses the reload, naming the field, the type that holds the view and the count, judged from the types that can hold such a view (as `[HR-47]`); a view the runtime cannot enumerate (`[HR-15a]`) that may point into such a part refuses it the same way. A row of `[HR-14]`: `a kept view points into a field that is removed, converted or rebuilt | refused ([HR-15c])`."
findings.milestone: M13 (M5 records which types hold views)

findings.title: A function value's state block has no schema: a captured value's type changes and the new body reads past the block
findings.why: [HR-13]: value data "is migrated through its container, which registers itself" — a state block is no container and registers nothing; [HR-15] names "function values' state held by any of these" only as a place whose *addresses* are rewritten; [HR-14]'s exhaustive table has no row for a lambda's captures; [HR-6a]: a function value's code word is the thunk, so the stored value runs the new body; [HR-45] gives generator frames exactly this protection and function values none.
findings.proposed_text: * `[HR-48]` *(new)* "**A function value keeps its state's layout.** The state of a lambda (`[CLO-10]`) has a schema: its captures as fields, with their words, and whether it fits in the state word. The runtime finds the live states of each reloadable lambda among the values it can enumerate (`[HR-15]`). A body change that leaves the captures and their types as they were applies through the thunk; a change to the captures, or a layout change of a captured value's type, is refused in plan while a state lives, naming the lambda (its function and line) and the count; a state the runtime cannot enumerate (kept by C, `[HR-20]`; behind a raw pointer, `[HR-13b]`) is treated as live. A row of `[HR-14]`: `a lambda's captures changed, or a captured value's type changed, while a state of it lives | refused ([HR-48])`." And in `[HR-41]`: `| a live function value's captures or a captured type changed | plan | refused ([HR-48]) |`.

findings.title: A function value stored by the old image stays in a place the new image's checks no longer count it in
findings.why: [EFF-2] (verdict 122): a call through a place has the effects of "every lambda and named function the program puts in that place" — a fact of the program's text, which a reload changes under values already stored. [HR-44] compares "a fact of a function that code the reload does not rebuild was checked against"; here the rebuilt code is what relies on a fact the running state contradicts, and "Code the reload rebuilds is checked again when it compiles, so a change that only it relies on is no refusal". No rule enumerates stored function values or callbacks C keeps against the new image's sets.
findings.proposed_text: * `[HR-44a]` *(new)* "**A stored function is a fact too.** Plan enumerates (`[HR-15]`) every function value held in a live instance, a registered container, a static or a lambda's state, and every callback C keeps (`[HR-20]`), and compares each with the functions the new image can put in that place (`[EFF-2]`, `[BLD-14]` point 7) or hand to C (`[FFI-52]`). Where a held function is not among them, the new image's checks of that place did not count it: the reload is refused (`E9030`), naming the place, the function and the count (\"`tree.on_visit` holds `prune` in 1 instance, which the new `setup` no longer stores there, and the new `walk` (line 8) walks `nodes` across its call; keep `prune` among what `setup` may store, or restart\"). A function value the runtime cannot enumerate is treated as held. Nothing of this runs while the program runs." And in `[HR-41]`: `| a stored function value or kept callback the new image does not count | plan | refused ([HR-44a]) |`.

findings.title: `OldSelf`'s fields that are themselves migrated types have no stated type: the old instance read with the new layout
findings.program:
class Log:
    name: String
    count: int                           # the edit adds `tag: u8 = 0` before `name`
class Audit:
    log: shares Log
    title: String
    static fn migrate_from(old: OldSelf) -> Result[Self, ReloadError]:
        return Ok(Audit(log=shares old.log, title=copy of old.log.name))   # <-- `old.log` is a view of the OLD `Log` instance; if its type in `OldAudit` is `shares Log`, `name` is read at the new offset of a block laid out the old way
findings.why: [HR-16]: "`OldSelf` is the previous schema as a generated struct `Old<Name>`, visible only in that function; `old` is a read-only view of the old instance" — the field types inside `Old<Name>` are unsaid, and so is whether a link read from `old` and stored in the new instance is the old target (then "applies the map" in [HR-2a] must rewrite it) or must be the new one.
findings.proposed_text: * `[HR-16]` append: "`Old<Name>`'s fields have the types of the previous schema: a field whose type is itself migrated in this reload is of that type's `Old` form (`log: shares OldLog`), through links, `owns` blocks, containers and tuples alike, so that nothing read through `old` is read with a new layout; a field whose type is unchanged keeps its type. An `Old` type has its fields and no methods. A `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared` or `weakref` link read from `old` may be stored into the new instance's field of the new type (`log=shares old.log`): it names the old instance until commit, and commit's map (`[HR-2a]`) repoints it to the migrated one; so `migrate_from` never reads the new instance of another type, and never stores a view of an `Old` value (`E3063`)."
findings.codes: E3063 for a stored Old view; otherwise text

findings.title: Commit does only pointer stores, prepare changes nothing, yet an instance migrates in place and reclaim ends its 'old version'
findings.program:
class Player:
    hp: int           # the edit: `hp: int` becomes `hp: i64` (widened, converted) and `name: String` is removed; the new size fits
    name: String
# [HR-15]: the instance keeps its address. [HR-2]: commit stores pointers into memory reserved in prepare: no byte of the old block is written there. [HR-2]/[HR-2a]: prepare "changes nothing" and builds the new instance "in the transaction arena". So who writes `hp`'s eight bytes into the old block, and where does reclaim find the old `name` to end after they were written?
findings.why: [HR-2]: "Commit performs only pointer stores into memory reserved in prepare"; "A failure in plan or prepare leaves the process ... with no instance changed"; [HR-15]: "Migration keeps an instance's address where the new size fits"; [HR-2a]: "Reclaim frees each migrated instance's old version field by field without the type's own `drop` ... and ends removed fields, running their `drop`" — an in-place instance has no old version left; and for a type rebuilt by `migrate_from` (whose `old` was only read) nothing says its carried-name fields are ended: a double end or a leak is the implementer's choice.
findings.proposed_text:
* `[HR-2]` replace "Commit performs only pointer stores into memory reserved in prepare: no allocation, check, callback or other fallible operation." with "Commit performs only stores: pointer stores into memory reserved in prepare, and, for an instance migrated in place (`[HR-15]`), the copy of its prepared bytes over its old block; no allocation, check, callback or other fallible operation."
* `[HR-2a]` replace the prepare and reclaim sentences with: "Prepare builds every migrated instance in the transaction arena (`[HR-37]`), an in-place one too, copies into the arena the old values of the fields that will not be carried over by name — removed fields, the old value of each converted field, and every field of an instance rebuilt by `migrate_from` — runs every `migrate_from` against a read-only view of the old instance, and computes the old-to-new address map; it writes nothing into an old block. ... Reclaim ends those saved old values, running their `drop`s and never the type's own `drop`, since the instance lives on in its new form; a field carried over by name has been handed over and is not ended; then it frees each old block whose instance moved."

findings.title: Field defaults, `Default.default()` and every function `migrate_from` calls run in prepare with ordinary panics
findings.why: [HR-14]: "field added with a default | initialised to that default", "field added, its type is `Default` | initialised to `Default.default()`"; [STR-2]: "A field default is any expression"; [HR-34]: "Prepare cannot panic"; [HR-35]: "every run-time check inside it ... returns `Err(...)`" and `E2225` for an explicit panic — both scoped to `migrate_from`'s own body; [HR-39] rejects a `noexcept` C++ call "at compile time" with no code. findings.title: A value made `using` an instance inside `migrate_from` comes from the transaction arena and is handed back to the wrong manager
findings.program:
static LEVEL: LevelArena = LevelArena(64 * 1024)
class Enemy:
    mesh: owns Mesh using LevelArena
    static fn migrate_from(old: OldSelf) -> Result[Self, ReloadError]:
        return Ok(Enemy(mesh=owns Mesh(points=copy of old.mesh.points) using LEVEL))   # <-- [HR-36]: "Allocation during prepare comes from the transaction arena": the block is the arena's, the value's instance word says LEVEL; its end hands LEVEL a block it never gave out. findings.why: [HR-36]: "Allocation during prepare comes from the transaction arena; ... construction inside `migrate_from` needs no special spelling"; [ALC-1]: a value "keeps its instance's address, one word, so that its growth and its end go back to the instance it came from"; [HR-46] keeps migrated values in their instance's block but says nothing of a value `migrate_from` makes anew; `old` is read-only, so the old `mesh` cannot be moved into the new instance.
findings.proposed_text: * `[HR-36]` append: "A value made `using` an instance (`[ALC-1]`) cannot come from the transaction arena, and a reload may not take memory from an instance it may discard: `using` in a `migrate_from` body, or in a default prepare runs, is `E2020` (\"`Mesh(...) using LEVEL` would take memory from `LEVEL` during a reload, which may be discarded; make the mesh in `Global` and give `mesh` no `using`, or let `Enemy` migrate by name\"), and a type that declares `migrate_from` and has a field whose type says `using A`, `A` a manager that may have several instances, is `E2020` at the `migrate_from` line (\"`Enemy.migrate_from` must build `mesh`, which takes its memory from a `LevelArena`, and a reload has no instance to take it from; remove `migrate_from` so that `mesh` is carried over by name (`[HR-46]`), or keep the mesh in `Global`\")."

findings.title: The live-instance list's synchronisation and a `thread_shared` object's reloadable header are unsaid
findings.program:
from std.thread import thread
class Job: pass
fn main():
    with scope = thread.scope():
        for i in 0..8:
            scope.spawn(owns fn(): Job())        # eight threads make objects at once: each insert links into "a live-instance list"
    g = thread_shared Job()
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared g: pass)   # <-- the other thread ends the last owner (after the hand-over, [RC-4] point 4) and must unlink `g` from the list while `main` inserts: with one list and no lock, a race; with per-thread lists, an unlink from another thread's list
findings.why: [HR-12]: "class instances are registered in a live-instance list, which adds 16 bytes to the object header of `[OBJ-1]` (24 bytes instead of 8, and 28 instead of 12 ...)": one list or one per thread, locked or not, is unsaid, and the 32-byte `thread_shared` header ([OBJ-1], verdict 101) has no reloadable size. [RT-11]: "no allocation updates a shared non-atomic counter" says nothing of the list. A wrong guess is a data race inside the runtime.

    unsafe:

[HR-13b]: "Value data reachable only through raw pointers ... cannot be migrated; if its schema changed, the reload is refused" — plan has no raw pointer to find, no count, and no rule saying it judges from types; a plan that enumerates what it can applies the change, and C's Vec2 is read with the new layout

Nothing refuses either call and nothing says how it is compiled.
verdicts.better_fix: The proposed text is right. Two amendments: say who compiles the copy of an instance across the edge in the same words `[BLD-14]` uses for generics ("whose body the instantiating package compiles"), so the two sentences agree; and make the refusal name the kind of callee: "`f(ref mut x, ref mut x)` names `x` twice, and `f` is a function value, which may hold any function, so no copy of it can be made for one variable; call the function by its name, `add_both(ref mut x, ref mut x)`, or give the second name a value of its own: `y = x` above the call and `f(ref mut x, ref mut y)`" — and the same `E3022` for an `extern` function ("`c_add(ref mut x, ref mut x)` names `x` twice, and `c_add` is C code, which has no copy for one variable").

verdicts.reason: [HR-3]: a reload is applied "only when no registered thread is executing Ember code (each thread's Ember-depth counter is zero)" — a condition at the moment commit reads the counters. [HR-6]: a thunk "loads the current target from the runtime's call table", written one slot at a time during commit, so the entering thread runs a mix of images over half-published instances.

(1) A thread that meets the mark must wait for the mark, not for the generation: when commit finds a counter that is not zero it "clears the mark and the poll returns `EMBER_RELOAD_UNSAFE_POINT`" and the generation never changes, so "waits until the reload generation counter changes" waits for ever; write "waits until the commit mark is cleared, and enters again". The `[COST-3]` row stands as proposed: entering Ember code from C in a reloadable build is one increment, one fence and one load; a thread waits only for the length of a commit it meets.
